messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette is missing some reported symptoms or demographic details. Rewrite it to include everything.

Previous vignette:
Eleanor has been a graphic designer for fifty years, and for most of that time, her home studio was a sanctuary of controlled, creative chaos. Now, at seventy-eight, it is a sterile, silent room. Six months ago, Hurricane Ida turned her world inside out, and she has been trying to put it back in order ever since. The storm had been an abstraction on the news until it was a physical monster trying to tear its way into her house. She and her husband, George, had stayed, certain they could ride it out like they had so many others. But this was different. The sound she remembers most, the one that lives in her ears still, was not the wind, but the violent, percussive slam of the back patio door as the frame splintered and the storm surge burst into their home. It slammed open, then shut, then open again, a frantic, splintering drumbeat against the roar of the water. With the flood came the smell of the marsh and something else, sharp and cloying—the contents of their liquor cabinet, shattered and mingling with the brackish water.

In the immediate aftermath, there was only shock. But as the weeks turned into months, the storm receded from the headlines but embedded itself in her nervous system. The sound of a door closing is no longer benign. When George comes home and shuts the front door, the solid click sends a jolt of pure terror through her. For a split second, she is not in her newly renovated hallway but back in the dark, water rising around her ankles, the memory so vivid it feels like it is happening right now, not something that is over. She can feel the cold water, smell the spilled gin. Other times, when she tries to explain this to George, the story comes out flat and distant. She can recite the events—the water level, the sound of their neighbor screaming for help, the long night waiting for rescue—with a profound numbness, as if she’s recounting a film she once saw about a stranger’s misfortune. It feels so extreme, so cinematic, that it’s hard for her to believe it actually happened to her.

Her life has become a series of strategic retreats. She spends hours at her computer, ostensibly working on a freelance logo design, but finds herself trapped in a loop, dwelling on how it all could have been prevented. If only they had left when the first warnings came. If only they had reinforced that back door. The thoughts circle endlessly, offering no comfort, only a confirmation of her own failure to protect them. This rumination is a constant, humming background noise to her days. To quiet it, she cleans. She organises her design software folders into labyrinthine sub-folders, wipes down her monitor and keyboard repeatedly, and arranges her pens by colour, then by size, then by colour again. This compulsive tidying is the only way she can exert a small measure of control over a world that now feels utterly, terrifyingly random and dangerous. She has come to believe that safety is an illusion. For seventy-eight years, she had believed in a certain kind of order, a fundamental fairness to the world. That belief has been completely destroyed, leaving a deep, unshakeable sense of injustice in its place. What happened was senseless and cruel, and nothing has been done to make it right.

The triggers are everywhere. The smell of alcohol is one of the worst. George has taken to drinking his nightly glass of bourbon on the porch, even in the cold, after she fled the living room one evening, gasping for air, because the scent transported her back to the flood. She avoids the news, clicking the television off the moment a reporter begins a story about loss or grief, the subject matter a raw nerve. These small avoidances have accumulated, carving out canyons between her and George, and between her and the world. It was after a particularly bad night, when the slam of a kitchen cabinet sent her into a full-blown panic where she crouched in the corner of her studio, that George insisted she seek help. Eleanor agreed, not because she believed it would work, but because she was exhausted. She is afraid she is losing her mind, that the storm didn’t just take her sense of security, but her very self. More than anything, she just wants to feel at home in her own house again, to believe that when a door closes, it is simply a door closing, and not the end of the world.

Missing items that MUST appear in the rewrite:
MISSING FROM VIGNETTE:
- Maladaptive Strategies: Memory Erasure: The vignette describes avoidance of external triggers and rumination about prevention, but it does not include any description of the patient actively trying to mentally erase or suppress the memory of the traumatic event itself.

---

Rewrite the full vignette (4–5 paragraphs, third person) incorporating all missing items as lived clinical experience.
Preserve all content from the previous vignette that was already correct — only add what is missing.
Do not use section headers or bullet points.
